item.title: Leo Terrell, Chair of the DOJ’s Task Force to Combat Antisemitism, took the stage at our Unite Against Extremism event with a message that couldn’t have been clearer: laws mean nothing if they are not enforced. Terrell called out a growing failure in major American cities to properly charge and prosecute hate crimes against Jews. At a time when Jewish Americans are being attacked in synagogues, targeted on their holidays, and harassed in everyday life simply because of who they are, the lack of consistent legal accountability is unacceptable. Los Angeles. New York. Boston. Chicago. These cities are seeing incidents, but too often not seeing consequences. Hate crimes are not symbolic offenses, they’re violations of civil rights. When they’re not regularly being prosecuted as such, it sends the dangerous message that violence against Jews can be minimized or ignored. Leo made clear that protecting civil rights requires action, prosecutors willing to bring charges, leaders willing to name the problem, and a system that treats violence against Jews with the seriousness it demands. The current wave of violence is not going to stop on its own. It must be met with real enforcement, real accountability, and real consequences instead of silence or excuses.
